content: Screening programs for hypertension and other non-communicable diseases, tuberculosis screening, and the provision of female condoms have been documented in the literature as part of integrated health services. Additionally, voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) has been implemented as an intervention for HIV prevention, often combined with family planning services and outreach efforts targeting high-risk communities. These integrated services have shown good uptake of VMMC. Since 2016, tetanus toxoid-containing vaccination (TTCV) has been recommended as an additional service to accompany VMMC to enhance safety and address gaps in tetanus immunity. This aligns with the 2017 WHO tetanus vaccine position paper, which emphasized the need for booster doses, particularly among adolescent boys. However, studies in Rwanda, Uganda, and Zambia have reported a significant decline in VMMC uptake when policies required two doses of TTCV prior to circumcision. In Uganda, more men dropped out after receiving the first TTCV dose when two doses were mandated compared to when only one dose was required, often administered on the same day as the circumcision (56% versus 99% circumcision completion rates). VMMC offers several benefits beyond HIV prevention for men who have sex with women, including reduced HIV risk for women and decreased risk of certain sexually transmitted infections (STIs). However, the procedure carries a small risk of adverse events (AEs), such as bleeding, infection, wound disruption, device displacement, and self-removal. Severe and moderate AEs are uncommon and manageable. Most circumcisions are performed using conventional surgical methods, such as the forceps-guided technique, under local anesthesia. However, AE definitions and severity classifications vary across studies, and follow-up intensity differs, making it challenging to generalize AE rates. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have demonstrated the safety of surgical male circumcision when performed under well-resourced research conditions by experienced surgeons or trained healthcare workers with expert supervision. These settings included close follow-up of clients over two years. However, such research conditions do not reflect routine service delivery environments. Since 2014, certain methods, such as the elastic collar compression device, have not been recommended for younger adolescents due to safety concerns. Data from country monitoring systems and WHO reports indicate that the most frequently reported severe AEs include excessive bleeding, infections, and rare cases of penile and glans injuries or urinary fistula. Between 2012 and 2018, 18 tetanus cases were reported post-VMMC. Surveillance systems, such as the United States President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), have also documented severe AEs, including bleeding, infections, glans injuries, urethral fistulae, and tetanus. Many of these events are resolvable, and AE rates may decline as programs mature and healthcare worker competence improves. Adequate tetanus vaccination among adolescent boys could further reduce tetanus risk. Psychological distress following circumcision has been minimally studied, with limited relevance to VMMC for HIV prevention. One case-control study in Turkey assessed psychosocial and physical effects after circumcision performed for unspecified reasons, not specifically for HIV prevention. There is no significant evidence of risk compensation behavior, such as increased risky sexual behavior, following circumcision. Extended post-trial follow-up of men in RCTs in Kenya and Uganda found little evidence of such behavior. However, continued attention to local contexts and accurate communication about partial protection and safer sexual practices is essential. The acceptability of VMMC is high among men and women, with many finding it acceptable for themselves, their partners, or their sons. Studies have identified facilitators for VMMC uptake, including increased knowledge of HIV/STI prevention, improved penile hygiene, and expectations of enhanced sexual activity or pleasure. However, barriers include fear of pain, potential complications, and time off work. Parental engagement and youth-friendly services are critical for encouraging adolescent participation and proper wound care post-surgery. Training for healthcare workers performing VMMC should include adolescent-specific guidance and address barriers such as negative interactions with healthcare workers and privacy violations. Additionally, incorporating elements of traditional non-medical circumcision into medical procedures may help address cultural preferences and improve service uptake.
